title: Book 9 — Calliope, Chapter 111
paragraphs: At last, however, as she continued to beg urgently and he was compelled by the rule — namely, that among them it is impossible for anyone who makes a request when a royal feast is laid before the king to fail to obtain it — he at last, very much against his will, consented. In handing her over, he told Amestris to do as she wished; meanwhile, he sent for his brother and said these words: “Masistes, you are the son of Darius and my brother, and in addition you are a man of worth. I tell you: live no longer with this wife you now live with. I give you instead my daughter; live with her as your wife, but do not keep the wife you now have — for it does not seem good to me that you should keep her.” Masistes, astonished at what was said, answered: “Master, how unprofitable is the speech you utter to me, in bidding me send away a wife by whom I have sons who are grown young men, and daughters — one of whom even you yourself took as wife for your son — and who is herself, as it happens, very much to my liking; that you bid me send her away and take to wife your daughter! I, O king, consider it a very great matter to be judged worthy of your daughter, but nevertheless I will do neither of these things. Do not compel me by force to do such a thing. For your daughter another husband will be found, in no way inferior to me; and let me, I beg you, still live with my own wife.” He answered with words something like these; and Xerxes, moved with anger, said: “This then, Masistes, is your case: I will not give you my daughter for your wife, nor shall you live any longer with that one — so that you may learn to accept what is offered to you.” On hearing this, he went out, saying first these words: “Master, surely you have not yet brought ruin upon me?”
